Commodious
kuh-MOH-dee-us
adj.
From Latin commodus (fit, convenient, suitable), through French commode; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Luke's account of Paul's hazardous sea voyage to Rome.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence.

Commodious appears once in the Authorized Version, in Luke's detailed, eyewitness account of Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner, describing the harbor of Fair Havens in Crete as not commodious, not suitable or convenient, for wintering the ship (Act 27:12). The practical decision that followed — sailing on toward a better harbor rather than remaining in an inadequate one — proved disastrous, as Luke records in careful nautical detail the violent tempestuous wind called Euroclydon that drove the ship for fourteen days before it finally ran aground and broke apart near Malta (Act 27:14-44). Paul had specifically warned against this decision, perceiving that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage (Act 27:10), a warning the centurion and shipmaster overruled in favor of the majority's judgment about the more commodious harbor. Yet the LORD had already promised Paul, through an angel that stood by him that night, that he must be brought before Caesar, and lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee (Act 27:23-24), a promise fulfilled exactly, every soul aboard surviving the wreck as foretold, demonstrating that God's providence secures His purposes even through, not merely despite, human misjudgment and genuine disaster.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from COMMODIOUS: convenient; suitable; affording ease or advantage; here of a harbor judged unsuitable for wintering a ship, a decision that led to shipwreck.

expand to see more

COMMODIOUS, adj. Convenient; suitable; affording ease, comfort, or advantage.

COMMODIOUS, adj. Roomy; spacious; well adapted to its purpose.

In Acts 27:12 the word describes a Cretan harbor judged unsuitable for wintering Paul's ship.

Paul had warned against sailing on, foreseeing 'hurt and much damage' (Act 27:10).

God's promise to Paul (Act 27:23-24) was fulfilled exactly despite the shipwreck that followed.

Key Scripture

Act 27:12 — "And because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence also, if by any means they might attain to Phenice, and there to winter; which is an haven of Crete, and lieth toward the south west and north west."

Modern Corruption

A fatalistic misreading could conclude that since God's promise was kept anyway, the majority's poor decision to sail did not matter, missing that Scripture holds both real human responsibility for bad judgment and God's sovereign faithfulness together without excusing the former.

expand to see more

The fact that God kept His promise to Paul despite the shipwreck does not erase the text's own verdict on the decision: Paul had rightly perceived the danger, and the majority's judgment, however reasonable it seemed, proved wrong and costly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the whole episode's demonstration of providence: God's purposes for Paul stood secure not because the voyage went smoothly but precisely through the storm and wreck, 'God hath given thee all them that sail with thee' (Act 27:24) fulfilled exactly as spoken.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Commodious occurs once, describing a Cretan harbor judged unfit for wintering Paul's ship, a decision to sail on that led to shipwreck yet did not thwart God's promise that every soul aboard would survive.

expand to see more

Commodious in Acts 27:12 describes a harbor judged unsuitable for wintering the ship.

The majority overruled Paul's warning of 'hurt and much damage' (Act 27:10) and sailed on.

The tempest Euroclydon drove the ship for fourteen days before it wrecked near Malta (Act 27:14-44).

An angel had promised Paul that all aboard would be saved (Act 27:23-24).

Every soul survived the wreck exactly as promised, demonstrating providence through disaster, not apart from it.

Usage

"Because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence."

"Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage (Act 27:10)."

"God hath given thee all them that sail with thee (Act 27:24) — the promise kept through the wreck."
